newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - MAY 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - MAY 14.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The finance ministry has once again turned to outstanding tax debts to boost flagging tax revenues in the first four months of the year. Under pressure to step up the pace of inflows, the ministry is dusting off an old provision that calls on about 350,000 taxpayers to wind up their outstanding affairs.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis will place the emphasis on finding relief for the unemployed in his address to the first meeting between government, unions and employers today on changes to the job market.

--The recent rate cuts by Alpha Credit Bank have led the finance ministry to a cut in the rate for annual Treasury bills, from 10.1 percent to 9.7 percent. Xiosbank followed Alpha Credit's lead yesterday, reducing lending and deposit interest rates.

--Despite the government's exhortations to speed up the procedures for the sale of the Elefsis Shipyards, the issue remains stalled due to the inability of creditor banks and the Social Security Foundation (IKA) to agree on issues.

--It took another seven years but the Athens Stock Exchange general price index jumped the 1,600 barrier yesterday. Trading was buoyant on the bourse, due in part to the recent announcement of rate cuts on deposit and lending accounts.
--Taxpayers will pay on average up to 49.6 percent more tax in comparison to 1995, according to reports. Meanwhile, seven tax officials will face court over charges of bribery and negligence.

--After Monday's announcement of rate cuts, Alpha Credit Bank is planning its next offensive in the housing credit market with reports that the administration is ready to establish a new subsidiary that will take advantage of all the privileges extended to specialised mortgage banks, including exemption from the 1.0 percent charge placed on all loans extended by commercial banks.

--The balance of current accounts has begun the year badly, with the Bank of Greece announcing a deficit of 21 million dollars for the first month of the year, compared to a surplus of 363.7 million dollars for the same month in 1996 and 720.6 million in January 1995.
--The International Monetary Fund has reportedly differed with the government on only one point - it wants the full deregulation of the job market and complete privatisations.
--Market sources said yesterday the finance ministry's decision to reduce rates on treasury bills was a bold move.
--A recent poll says that most Greeks believe that an institutional framework for job relations is non-existent, as social dialogue on changes to the labour market kicks off today.

--The prime minister is expected today to announce the inclusion of social security issues on the agenda of social dialogue between government, unions and employers. If social security and pension issues are included it will widen the circle of participants in the social dialogue.
